To tell a story on three levels: setting, action, what had happened before.
Grandma Rosario has cooked cocido for Sunday. On Sunday morning, the pot is empty. Ana plays detective.
It can’t be! Yesterday afternoon I had made a huge pot of cocido. And now it’s empty!
Calm down, Grandma. We’ll find the culprit. Who was in the house last night?
Pablo came at nine, but when I went to bed, at ten, he had already left.
Pablo, what did you do last night?
Me? Nothing. I came to bring Grandma some medicine. I had already had dinner at home.
Hmm… And you, Mihai, where were you?
At the hospital, on call. I got home at seven in the morning. I had never worked so many hours in a row!
But you have a key to this house… And you’ve got a tomato stain on your shirt.
That’s from the hospital! I had eaten a sandwich before my shift.
Grandma, had you closed the kitchen door?
I don’t think so… Oh no! And the window was open.
(looking at the floor) Look: small footprints… with four toes. And breadcrumbs all the way to the garden.
It’s Coco, the neighbour’s dog! This morning I had seen him looking very happy!
That dog! Oh well, today we’re having tortilla. And next time, I’m closing the window!

English has the past perfect: “I had eaten”, “it had left”. Spanish forms it like the perfecto (chapter 13), but with HABER in the imperfect, just as English uses “had”:
The participles are the same as for the perfecto: the irregular hecho, visto, dicho, vuelto, escrito, abierto, puesto, roto.
2. When to use it: “the past of the past”
You have a moment in the past (the reference point). The pluscuamperfecto shows what had already happened BEFORE that moment.
When I got to the station, the train had already left.
When I went to bed, Pablo had already left.
I didn’t go to the cinema because I had already seen the film.
Draw a timeline: NOW ← the past moment (indefinido) ← what was already done before (pluscuamperfecto).
Nunca había comido algo tan rico.
“Nunca había…” is perfect for a first experience: “¡Nunca había visto algo así!” = I’d never seen anything like it!
A simple way to order actions without complicated tenses: antes de / después de + INFINITIVE (the dictionary form of the verb).
Before going out, I closed the window.
After dinner (after eating), we watched a film.
I brush my teeth before going to bed.
Don’t conjugate the verb after “antes de / después de”: “antes de salir”, not “antes de salí”. Where English uses “-ing” (before leaving), Spanish uses the infinitive.
5. A story with three past tenses
Now you have all four past tenses of the A2 level. Here’s how they work together in a story:
Alguien se había comido el cocido.
Desde entonces, siempre he cerrado la ventana.
If you can use all four correctly, you’ve got past one of the hardest parts of Spanish grammar. ¡Enhorabuena!

Lena tells the story of her driving test day. Pay attention to the order of events!
On the day of my driving test I woke up late. The night before I hadn’t slept at all because of nerves.
When I looked at the clock, it was half past eight. The test was at nine!
I got dressed quickly and ran out. On the metro I realised I had left my ID card at home.
I went back to get it. When I got to the test centre, the examiner had already called everyone else.
“You’re late,” he told me. “I’m very sorry,” I answered, “I had forgotten my ID card.”
Luckily, he let me take the test last.
I was so nervous that, before setting off, I had already stalled the engine twice.
But after a few minutes I calmed down. I drove well, parked perfectly and didn’t make a single mistake.
At the end, the examiner smiled and said: “Passed.”
I had never been so happy. And I had never been so late for anything!
to drive (“examen de conducir” = driving test)
previous (“la noche anterior” = the night before)
No había dormido por los nervios
Había apagado el motor dos veces
In February, something strange was happening in the A&E staff room at the hospital.
Every night, someone was eating the sandwiches that the doctors and nurses had left in the fridge.
The first victim was Pilar. She had lovingly made herself a tortilla sandwich. When she opened the fridge at three in the morning, only the paper was left.
A week later, Dr García’s jamón sandwich disappeared. Then Mihai’s cheese one.
Everyone was annoyed. The head of A&E put a sign on the fridge: “To the sandwich thief: we’re watching you.”
But the thief carried on. Nobody had ever seen him.
Mihai decided to investigate. One night, before starting his shift, he made a special sandwich: with lots and lots of hot chilli. Then he left it in the fridge and waited.
At four in the morning he heard a scream in the corridor. He ran to the staff room.
There was the medical student, Daniel, red as a tomato, drinking water straight from the tap.
On the table was Mihai’s sandwich, with a single bite out of it.
Daniel looked at Mihai, ashamed. There was no doubt now: he had found the thief.
“I’m so, so sorry,” said Daniel. He explained that he had moved to Madrid in January and had no money. His grant hadn’t arrived yet.
For weeks he had been eating only what he could find. He was so ashamed that he hadn’t told anyone.
Mihai remembered his first year in Madrid, when he didn’t have much either. He didn’t get angry.
The next day he talked to his colleagues. They organised something lovely: every night, someone would bring an extra sandwich “for the student”.
In March, Daniel’s grant finally arrived. The first thing he did was buy cakes for the whole A&E team.
In the box there was a note: “Thank you for feeding the thief. I promise not to steal any more… except Mihai’s spicy sandwiches, which made me cry.”
Today Daniel is a doctor. He works at the same hospital as Mihai. And every time a new student arrives, he leaves an extra sandwich in the fridge, with a note: “For you. No chilli”.
Mihai sometimes sees him from the doorway and smiles. Some traditions start with a theft.
And Pilar can finally eat in peace.
¿Qué hizo Daniel cuando llegó su beca?
